claims.text: Laser-assisted reactive synthesis will enable a large-scale reaction between RHEA constituents and Cu.
Laser-assisted reactive synthesis will suppress diffusion-driven segregation in an RHEA-Cu composite.
The proposed process will produce a stable, homogeneous RHEA-Cu composite microstructure.
Advanced free-energy sampling can be used to guide processing parameters for a multicomponent refractory alloy.
Advanced free-energy sampling can identify the non-equilibrium reaction landscape and processing window for an RHEA-Cu reaction.
The starting material can consist of refractory-element powders or pre-alloyed RHEA feedstock mixed with Cu powders.
A positive heat of mixing between the RHEA constituents and Cu causes phase segregation during traditional processing.
High heating rates and controlled cooling can kinetically drive the desired reaction while suppressing equilibrium segregation.
Next-generation reactor materials must tolerate high temperature and irradiation conditions.
The laser processing conditions can mimic both the thermal and irradiation environments of next-generation reactors.
Microstructure formation at the RHEA-Cu interface is sensitive to phase-formation and segregation kinetics.
Rapid heating increases kinetic energy and drives the RHEA-Cu reaction before significant diffusion occurs.
Controlled cooling kinetically traps a metastable, homogeneous RHEA-Cu interface.
Rapid heating and controlled cooling counteract the thermodynamic drive for RHEA-Cu phase segregation.
The resulting large-scale RHEA-Cu composite will have strong interfacial bonding.
Standard powder metallurgy or simple blending tends to produce phase segregation and an unstable RHEA-Cu interface.
Successful scale-up depends on maintaining a precisely controlled non-equilibrium heating and cooling window.
The heating rate, cooling rate, laser energy density, and reaction time needed to suppress segregation are not yet known.
